property_summary: For every valid call to transfer by the authorized from-address, the reference contract always returns true (call succeeds and returns true); the mutant returns false for the same successful executions, breaking this property for some inputs.

For any non-empty _tos array and matching v array provided by the authorized caller, C.transfer(...) returns true; the mutant returns false for some such inputs, so the property asserts that the call's returned boolean is true.

For every non-empty _tos array and corresponding v array called by the authorized sender, C.transfer(...) returns true (the reference always returns true on successful execution), whereas the mutant returns false for some such inputs, so the test asserts the call-return is true.

For any non-empty _tos and v arrays called by the authorized sender and where the external low-level calls to caddress do not revert, the reference C.transfer returns true (call succeeds and returns true); the mutant returns false for the same inputs — so the property is that a successful external-interaction invocation of transfer returns true.

For any non-empty arrays _tos and v invoked by the authorized sender with a callee that always succeeds, C.transfer(...) returns true (the reference always returns true on successful completion), whereas the mutant returns false for those same successful invocations.

For any inputs, the reference C.transfer never returns false when the external low-level calls to caddress fail (it always returns true if it doesn't revert); the mutant returns false as soon as any low-level call returns false, so there exist inputs (when the callee returns false) that make the mutant return false while the reference still returns true.

For every call to transfer with any list of recipients and amounts, the reference C never returns false (it returns true as long as it doesn't revert), but the mutant may return false if any external low-level call to caddress returns false; the test deploys a callee that intentionally returns false for a chosen index so the mutant will differ.

For every input, the reference C.transfer never returns false (it returns true whenever it doesn't revert); the mutant can return false if an external low-level call returns false, so deploying a callee that returns false for some entry will make the mutant disagree while the reference still returns true.

For any inputs, the reference contract's transfer(...) never returns false (it always returns true when it does not revert); the mutant may return false if an external low-level call to caddress returns false, so a callee that returns false for some call will make the mutant differ while the reference still returns true.

For every admissible input, C.transfer(...) (reference) never returns false (it returns true whenever it doesn't revert); the mutant may return false if an external low-level call to caddress returns false, so deploying a callee that returns false for some calls will make the mutant return false while the reference still returns true.

For any caller and inputs, the reference contract only allows transfers when msg.sender equals the original owner address (0x9797...6c9); the mutant requiring a different caller violates this by allowing the transfer call to succeed only when msg.sender equals the other address, so there exist callers for which behavior differs (i.e., whether transfer call succeeds), which the test detects by fuzzing the caller address.

For any caller address and non-empty arrays of equal length, the reference C only allows transfer to be called successfully when msg.sender == from (the stored owner); the mutant requiring a different hardcoded sender will cause calls from that owner to revert (or succeed only for the other address), so there exists a caller for which behavior differs — we assert that calling transfer as the contract's public `from` succeeds for all admissible inputs.

For every admissible inputs, calling transfer(...) on the correct contract C always returns true (completes without revert) because multiplying v[i] by 1e18 via mul_uint256 keeps the arithmetic path safe, while the mutant that computes mul_uint256(v[i] / 1, 1e18) can cause a different revert/behavior for some inputs (due to different arithmetic path / division semantics) and thus may make transfer revert (i.e., not complete successfully) for some fuzzed inputs and adversarial callee behavior.

For every admissible input, calling transfer(...) on the correct contract C always completes successfully (does not revert) even when the callee reverts; the mutant's change to use v[i] / 1 before multiplication can change execution path and cause the call to revert for some input and adversarial callee, so the mutant fails the universal non-revert property for some fuzzed inputs.

For every admissible input where caller is the authorized from and _tos.length>0, the reference C.transfer(...) always returns true (completes without revert) even if a callee reverts; the mutant's change (using v[i] / 1 before mul) can cause a different execution path that makes transfer revert for some fuzzed v and a reverting callee.

For every caller equal to the authorized sender and any non-empty _tos with a callee that always reverts, the reference C.transfer(...) never reverts (it swallows/ignores callee failures because arithmetic path keeps mul_uint256 from reverting), while the mutant can revert for some fuzzed v when interacting with a reverting callee due to the changed arithmetic path (v[i] / 1) altering overflow/division behavior and causing a revert for some input.

For any caller equal to the authorized sender and any non-empty _tos, C.transfer(...) always returns true (does not revert) when some callee address in _tos points to a contract that reverts on calls; the mutant's change (using v[i] / 1 before multiplication) can make transfer revert for some fuzzed v and a reverting callee.

For all inputs, the reference contract requires that the _tos array is non-empty, so calling transfer(...) with an empty _tos array will revert (fail); the mutant removes that require and will instead succeed and return true for empty arrays, violating the rule.

For any inputs, the reference contract C always makes the low-level external calls to its immutable caddress (so calling transfer never triggers a call to msg.sender and thus never observes msg.sender-side effects); the mutant that replaces caddress with msg.sender can instead invoke code at the caller and therefore can make transfer revert by using a malicious caller — so the rule is: transfer(...) on the correct C never reverts when called by the authorized caller (it always returns true), but the mutant can be forced to revert for some caller that is a malicious contract.

For all inputs where msg.sender is the authorized caller and the tos array has at least one element, the reference C.transfer(...) always returns true (does not revert) because it calls a fixed caddress; the mutant that calls msg.sender can be made to revert by making msg.sender a malicious contract whose fallback reverts, so the property is: transfer(...) always succeeds (returns true) for the authorized sender — the mutant violates this for some adversarial caller.

For any fuzzed _tos and v (with _tos.length>0 and caller equal to the authorized address), the reference C.transfer(...) always returns true (does not revert) because it calls a fixed caddress; the mutant that calls msg.sender can be made to revert for some malicious caller contract, so the rule is that transfer(...) never reverts for the authorized EOA caller while the mutant can be forced to revert when the caller is a malicious contract.

For any non-empty _tos array and caller equal to the authorized address, calling transfer(...) on the reference C always returns true (does not revert) even if the caller is a contract with a reverting fallback because C calls a fixed caddress; the mutant that calls msg.sender can be made to revert for some malicious caller contract, breaking this property.

For any caller equal to the authorized address and any non-empty inputs, the reference C.transfer(...) always returns true (does not revert) because it calls a fixed external caddress; the mutant that calls msg.sender can be made to revert when the caller is a malicious contract, so the property is that transfer(...) never reverts for the authorized caller — the mutant violates this for some adversarial caller contract.

For any non-empty array of recipient addresses and corresponding uint amounts, the reference contract always passes to the external caddress.transferFrom call amounts that are exactly v[i] * 1e18, whereas the mutant omits the 1e18 scaling and thus for some fuzzed v[] will produce a different value observed via the callee; we detect this by deploying a helper that records the last amount seen and asserting the helper always saw amounts scaled by 1e18 after calling c.transfer.

For any caller and parallel arrays _tos and v (non-empty and same length), the reference C always calls its caddress with transferFrom amounts equal to v[i] * 1e18 (scaled by 1e18); the mutant omits the scaling and therefore for some fuzzed v the callee will observe an amount not equal to v[i]*1e18.

For any non-empty arrays _tos and v called by the authorized sender, C always calls its external caddress with transferFrom amounts equal to v[i] * 1e18 for each i; the mutant omits the 1e18 scaling, so a deployed callee that records the observed amounts will sometimes see values not equal to v[i]*1e18 and thus violate the property.

For every admissible input (authorized caller, non-empty _tos and matching v lengths), the reference C always calls its external caddress.transferFrom with amounts equal to v[i] * 1e18; the mutant omits the multiplication and thus for some fuzzed v values the callee will observe a different amount, breaking the property.

For any non-empty arrays of recipients and amounts called by the authorized sender, contract C always forwards amounts scaled by 1e18 to its caddress (i.e., it calls transferFrom with amount == v[i] * 1e18 for each i); the mutant omits this scaling and so for some fuzzed v the observed forwarded amount differs, breaking the property.
